I had the good fortune to meet my dear professor and brother, Dr. Mostafa Tajzadeh, during his leave, on the night before his return to Evin Prison. He was deeply worried about the economic pressure facing the people and warned about the need to safeguard the collective psyche of society, urging every effort to prevent civil war in the country. He continued to regard a return to the people's vote as the central solution to the country's conflicts, and described the order of all political, social, and cultural affairs as contingent upon this. His spirit was resolute, his lips smiling, his eyes bright, his memory sharp, his morale excellent, and his composure intact — and his mind was still swiftly working through interdisciplinary issues. I explained to him what I had envisioned regarding the perspective, and I entrusted him and his dear family to God the Merciful. The sound of Mr. Mostafa's laughter still echoes in my ears through the darkness of this pitch-black night.@yaser_arab57

Request for brainstorming. Hello dear ones. Without further ado, the suicide situation in our country (based on scattered information!) needs to be raised and brought into the circle of the country's issues. Moving toward instances and sensational, hot headlines, and adding fuel to the fire, does not cure any pain. Apparently, news agencies have also been banned from covering suicide news, which, given the expanse of social networks, is a futile measure. My belief is that we need a problem-oriented dialogue in this area. But three considerations have given me pause, and I need your intellectual help. One: How can the very act of talking about recent suicides not itself lead to inflaming this issue in the public mind? (What considerations should be taken into account?) Two: What should we title the session so that the subject is clear and it does not seem irrelevant or too general? Three: Should those who have attempted suicide also be invited, and should we also listen to their views? Or should only experts and researchers be present? I would appreciate it if you would send me your opinions.👇@Arab_Yaser@yaser_arab57

At the meeting to discuss issues in education in Iran, we first put some of the problems and challenges facing the education system on the table in a collective discussion, using brainstorming. In the second step, friends shared their experiences and suggestions, including Mr. Morteza Kia, one of the leading figures and activists in the field of humanities and the former director of the specialized humanities school, who spoke about what education can do. But in the third step, we want to look at the issue from a different angle: what can people and civil institutions do to help education today, without waiting for all structures to be reformed? In this part, Mr. Sadegh Keshavarzian speaks about the experience and idea of forming the "Alef-B" NGO and the possibility of practical intervention and help by society in education, especially in deprived areas. He is showing the audience a path on which one can work on empowering teachers without government support. A path that he and his friends have traveled for several years, and so far they have empowered hundreds of teachers, especially in deprived areas. Source: @yaser_arab57

Coca-Cola and cherry compote! That's how down-to-earth Morteza's remarks began... Mr. Morteza Kia is among the elites in the field of humanities; he earned a single-digit or double-digit rank on the university entrance exam and is currently a PhD student in law at the University of Tehran. He has served as principal of a specialized humanities high school for years, and I too have had the privilege of collaborating with him in the field of education and the practical application of the humanities. (A high school that was shut down because it was not recognized among the schools!) In this short presentation, Mr. Kia points to a very important matter: the way out for the country's education system does not necessarily pass through increasing the budget; rather, the very role and proprietorship of the government in running schools must be reconsidered. Today, a significant portion of discussions about the problems of the education system revolves around the issue of budget. That if more budget is allocated to education, the quality of education will also increase. But what Mr. Kia raises in this presentation brings up another matter: an important part of the problem is not merely the shortage of resources, but the manner of the governance's proprietorship over education and the direct administration of schools. In this same short presentation, he puts several specific solutions on the table and shows that the relationship between the government, the school, and educational management can be thought about differently. He shows where the bulk of the money of non-governmental schools goes? He shows why our principals are typically procurement officers rather than managers? He shows how the legal structure of education creates double standards? @yaser_arab57 Full conversation https://www.aparat.com/v/ilzfq26
